docs.title: ucode-prometheus-exporter
docs.text:
Metrics of OpenWrt for Prometheus, written in ucode and served by uhttpd at /metrics on port 9100. It replaces the packages feed's prometheus-node-exporter-ucode and prometheus-node-exporter-lua, with the Lua exporter's collectors ported alongside the ucode one's, under names of its own: the package ucode-prometheus-exporter, the service, command and configuration prometheus-exporter.

apk add ucode-prometheus-exporter ucode-prometheus-exporter-full
wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:9100/metrics
  • node_exporter's names. Where the Prometheus node_exporter has a metric, the exporter writes its name, type, labels and help, so dashboards made for it work. Elsewhere, the Prometheus naming conventions.
  • A collector per package. The base package has what every device can use; each other collector is a package of its own, and groups install several at once.
  • A jail built from what the collectors declare. uhttpd runs the exporter in procd's jail, which holds what the installed collectors need and nothing else.
  • Nothing to observe is not a failure. A device without radios, or with dnsmasq disabled, is not failing to read them.
  • A ubus object and a LuCI app. Ask the exporter what it would do, from a script or from LuCI.

It targets OpenWrt 25.12 and uses no ucode API newer than that release's. Apache License 2.0.

docs.title: Renamed Metrics
docs.text:
This exporter replaces OpenWrt's prometheus-node-exporter-ucode and prometheus-node-exporter-lua (it conflicts with both, and takes over their settings), but not their metric names. Where the Prometheus node_exporter has an equivalent metric, this exporter uses node_exporter's name, type, labels and help text, so dashboards made for it (such as Grafana's "Node Exporter Full") work. Elsewhere, the names follow the Prometheus naming conventions:

  • base units in the name (_seconds, _bytes, _hertz, _bits_per_second, _celsius, _ratio, and _dbm or _db for radio levels);
  • _total on counters only, and every counter ends in _total;
  • a metric of labels only is <name>_info with the value 1;
  • a boolean is a gauge of 0 or 1, an enumeration one series per state with the value 1 or 0;
  • snake_case metric and label names, and no unit on a unitless value.

Each service keeps its own prefix (dnsmasq_, dsl_, wireguard_, mwan3_, hostapd_, dawn_, bmx7_, realtek_poe_, ubnt_, modemmanager_, unbound_, nft_counter_), and OpenWrt's own metrics are node_openwrt_*. Where a widely used standalone exporter exists for a service and its names follow the conventions, this exporter uses them too: see Standalone exporters.

There is no option to get the old names back. The table below lists, per collector, every family whose name, type, labels or unit changed, from the names of the exporters this one replaces to this one's; a family not listed has kept its name. In the Type column, a → b is a type that changed.

Every family as the collectors write it now is in Metrics; why the names are what they are, in About metric names.

docs.title: New metrics
docs.text:
Neither upstream exporter had these. Where node_exporter has the metric, the name, type, labels and help are its own.

Collector Families Type Source — (the exporter's own) ucode_prometheus_exporter_build_info{version} gauge 1, labeled with the package's version (0.1.0-r1, dev from a source tree), in every scrape whatever collect[] selects; it succeeds without samples), 1 for every other; see About nothing to observe. conntrack (base) node_nf_conntrack_stat_{found,invalid,ignore,insert,insert_failed,drop,early_drop,search_restart} gauge node_exporter's, from /proc/net/stat/nf_conntrack summed over the CPUs. softnet (base) node_softnet_{processed,dropped,times_squeezed,cpu_collision,received_rps,flow_limit_count}_total{cpu} counter node_exporter's, from /proc/net/softnet_stat. softnet (base) node_softnet_backlog_len{cpu} gauge node_exporter's. vmstat (base) node_vmstat_<field> (default fields: oom_kill, pgpg*, pswp*, pg*fault*; option fields) untyped node_exporter's, from /proc/vmstat. openwrt_interfaces (base) node_openwrt_interface_{up,pending,available,autostart}{interface} gauge netifd's network.interface dump, 0 or 1. openwrt_interfaces (base) node_openwrt_interface_uptime_seconds{interface} gauge netifd's uptime, while the interface is up. openwrt_interfaces (base) node_openwrt_interface_info{interface,proto,device,l3_device} gauge 1; a label netifd does not report is left out. openwrt_interfaces (base) node_openwrt_interface_addresses{interface,family}, node_openwrt_interface_routes{interface,family} gauge Counts: an address as a label would change with every WAN lease. openwrt_interfaces (base) node_openwrt_interface_ipv6_prefixes{interface}, node_openwrt_interface_errors{interface} gauge Delegated prefixes; the errors netifd holds for the interface. dhcp_leases node_openwrt_dhcp_leases{server,interface,family} gauge Active leases of dnsmasq (its lease file) and odhcpd (ubus call dhcp ipv4leases/ipv6leases). dhcp_leases (option leases) node_openwrt_dhcp_lease_info{server,interface,family,address,mac,duid,iaid,hostname}, node_openwrt_dhcp_lease_expiry_timestamp_seconds{server,interface,family,address} gauge A series per lease; docs.title: About the Exporter
docs.text: ucode-prometheus-exporter serves the metrics of an OpenWrt device to Prometheus: its CPU, memory, network devices and connections, and the services a router runs, from Wi-Fi to WireGuard to DNS. It is written in ucode, OpenWrt's own scripting language, and served by uhttpd, the web server every OpenWrt image already has. This page is about where it comes from, and why it is a rewrite rather than a patch.

docs.title: Two exporters before it
docs.text:
OpenWrt's packages feed has had two Prometheus exporters, both Apache-2.0.

prometheus-node-exporter-lua came first, in 2017. Christian Simon added it; Etienne Champetier maintains it, and split its single script into the collectors it has today. Over the years contributors added collectors for nearly everything a router does: Wi-Fi stations, hostapd, DSL modems, PoE switches, mesh daemons, mwan3, ModemManager, Ubiquiti radios, Unbound.

prometheus-node-exporter-ucode followed in 2022, by Andre Heider, who maintains it. It is the same idea in ucode, which OpenWrt had by then made its language of choice: LuCI's backend and the firewall, fw4, are ucode, and rpcd takes plugins in it. It has the core collectors and a handful of extras, and needs no Lua.

Between them, the ground was covered twice and unevenly: most collectors existed in Lua only, a few in ucode only, and some in both with different names. A device that wanted the Lua exporter's breadth needed a Lua runtime, which an image built around ucode otherwise does without.

docs.title: Why a rewrite
docs.text:
This exporter ports the Lua exporter's collectors alongside the ucode one's, so every collector either had is here, in ucode. Writing them anew, rather than translating them line by line, let every collector take the same shape, built for three things a router asks of code that runs as root on it: to touch only what it must, to be tested before it gets there, and to be fast on a MIPS CPU.

  • Each collector says what it touches. A collector declares the capabilities it needs, the configs it reads and the programs it runs, and gets those and nothing else. The service builds its jail from those declarations: see About the security model.
  • Everything is tested off the device. Only one module touches the system; the tests hand collectors fakes of it, fed by what real devices answered. A collector is tested on the captures of real routers before it ever runs on one.
  • It is fast where it matters. A typical router's full scrape takes about two seconds on a MIPS CPU of 500 MIPS, the class of an MT7621. See Performance on small routers.
  • It says what it cannot observe. A device without radios is not failing to read its radios. See About nothing to observe.
  • The metric names are node_exporter's. Dashboards made for node_exporter work as they are. See About metric names.

The names are the change that costs the most: queries made for either feed exporter break. A rewrite is the time to pay that once, rather than have every later version carry two sets of names.

docs.title: Why not node_exporter itself
docs.text: The Prometheus node_exporter runs on Linux, and some run it on OpenWrt. It is a Go binary of several megabytes, a lot on a router with 16 MB of flash, and it knows nothing of what makes a device an OpenWrt router: netifd's interfaces, hostapd, ubus, uci. This exporter takes node_exporter's names, so it fits the same dashboards, and adds what only OpenWrt has. Its base package is about 65 kB, and what it depends on, ucode and uhttpd, an image with LuCI mostly has already.

docs.title: Replacing, not sitting beside
docs.text: It installs under names of its own, ucode-prometheus-exporter and the prometheus-exporter service, and conflicts with both feed exporters: they all want port 9100 and uhttpd's /metrics. When it is installed where one of them was, it takes over that one's settings. See How to move from the feed's exporters.

docs.title: Credits
docs.text:
The collectors port those of the two feed packages: prometheus-node-exporter-ucode, by Andre Heider and contributors, and prometheus-node-exporter-lua, by Jeff Schornick, Kevin Lyda, Christian Simon, Etienne Champetier and contributors. NOTICE credits each collector's upstream authors.

Metric names and help texts follow the Prometheus node_exporter and, for Unbound, WireGuard and chrony, unbound_exporter, prometheus_wireguard_exporter and chrony_exporter. Tests run on utest.

docs.title: About the Architecture
docs.text: The exporter is not a daemon. It is a handler that uhttpd runs, a library of modules, a ubus object that rpcd serves, and an init script that ties them to procd. This page is about how those pieces fit, and why they are cut where they are.

docs.title: The pieces
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    P[Prometheus] -- "GET /metrics" --> U
    subgraph jail[procd's jail]
        U[uhttpd] --> H[handler.uc]
        H --> L[collectors]
    end
    L -- "deps: fs, ubus, uci, netlink, exec" --> S[(the system)]
    R[rpcd] --> O[ubus object prometheus-exporter]
    O --> LuCI
    O -.-> X[rpc-status.uc]
    I[init script] -- "jail.uc: mounts" --> jail
  • uhttpd and the handler. /usr/libexec/prometheus-exporter/handler.uc is a uhttpd-mod-ucode handler for /metrics. uhttpd is the server every OpenWrt image has; it does TLS, keep-alive and the socket work, and the exporter never listens on anything itself.
  • The library. /usr/share/ucode/prometheus_exporter/ holds the modules the handler, the command line, check and the ubus object share: the loader, the configuration, the scrape, the exposition format, the jail's rules.
  • The collectors. One module each, in collectors/, installed by the base package or a package of its own.
  • The ubus object. rpcd serves prometheus-exporter from a ucode plugin. It is how LuCI, or a script, asks the exporter what it would do: which collectors are installed, whether a value is valid, how each collector does.
  • The init script. It checks the configuration, works out the jail from what the collectors declare, and hands procd the uhttpd instance.

docs.title: A process per request
docs.text:
uhttpd-mod-ucode runs the handler once, when uhttpd starts, and then answers each request in a process forked from that one. Everything the handler did at load time is there in every request, already done: the collectors are compiled and validated once, the configuration's compress and basic auth are read once. Nothing a request does is there for the next: its memory goes with its process.

That shapes two choices.

The first is that loading is the place for anything costly that does not change between scrapes, and that a change of what was loaded needs a restart, not a reload. Installing a collector package reloads the service; the init script has procd watch every collector module and config the jail mounts, and procd restarts uhttpd when one changed.

The second is that what must outlast a request has to go to disk. The one thing that does is basic auth's cache: checking a password against its hash costs a scrape a large share of its time on a slow CPU, and a cache in memory would be gone by the next request. So each uhttpd instance has a small state directory on tmpfs, the one path its jail mounts read-write, and its files are named after the instance. The handler names its instance when uhttpd loads it, by the pid and start time of that process, which no later process can share; and it removes every other instance's files then. A restart starts without state, which is what a changed password or a changed collector should mean anyway.

docs.title: Only one module touches the system
docs.text:
prometheus_exporter.deps is the only module that imports fs, ubus, uci, rtnl, nl80211 and socket. A collector does not import them: it declares in meta.needs the capabilities it wants, and collect receives exactly those, in its deps argument.

This is dependency injection, and it pays three times.

  • Tests. A test builds deps from utest's mocks, fed with what real devices answered, and runs the collector as a scrape would. No collector needs a router to be tested.
  • The jail. What a collector may reach is written down, so the service can build the jail from it rather than from a list someone keeps by hand.
  • The narrowing. deps is not the module, but a channel over it that hands out less: fs without its writing functions, uci as handles on the configs a collector named and nothing else, read-only and of the committed configuration only, exec only for the programs listed and with a deadline. A collector that tries more has no way to.

Taking every native function by name in one module also makes make lint meaningful: loading that module on OpenWrt 25.12's ucode fails if the release lacks a function the exporter uses, at build time and not in a scrape.

docs.title: The loader
docs.text: The loader takes every module of the collectors' directory, validates its meta and collect, and leaves out one that does not load or is not valid, logging why. A broken subpackage costs its own collector and nothing else. The same loader runs in the handler, the command line, check, the jail's script and the ubus object, so all of them agree on what is installed.

docs.title: Why the ubus object lives in rpcd
docs.text:
The handler only runs inside a request, and only in the jail. Something has to answer questions about the exporter when nobody scrapes, outside the jail, and to LuCI: rpcd, which every image runs, and which already serves LuCI's other objects. Its plugin reads with the exporter's own modules, so it sees what the exporter sees.

One method, status, runs a scrape. Collectors call ubus objects, and some of those objects are rpcd's own (wireguard, luci): rpcd cannot answer them while it waits for the scrape. So status runs the scrape in a process of its own and replies when that process is done, and rpcd answers other calls meanwhile.

docs.title: About Metric Names
docs.text: The metric names are not those of the feed's exporters. They are the Prometheus node_exporter's where it has the metric, and elsewhere follow the Prometheus naming conventions. This page is about why, and about the one name the exporter writes of itself.

docs.title: node_exporter's names first
docs.text: Where node_exporter has a metric, this exporter uses its name, type, labels and help text: node_cpu_seconds_total{cpu="0",mode}, not the cpu="cpu0" the feed's exporters wrote; node_wifi_* with device and mac_address, not wifi_* with ifname and mac. The point is the ecosystem around node_exporter: dashboards such as Grafana's "Node Exporter Full", recording rules and alerts written for Linux hosts all work on a router without a single edit. A router is a Linux host, and its CPU, memory, disks and network devices should look like one.

docs.title: The conventions elsewhere
docs.text:
Most of what a router has, node_exporter does not: netifd's interfaces, DHCP leases, hostapd's stations, DSL lines, PoE ports. Those follow the Prometheus naming conventions:

  • base units in the name: _seconds, _bytes, _hertz, _bits_per_second, _celsius, _ratio, and _dbm or _db for radio levels;
  • _total on counters only, and every counter ends in _total;
  • a metric of labels only is <name>_info, with the value 1;
  • a boolean is a gauge of 0 or 1; an enumeration, one series per state;
  • snake_case names, and no unit on a unitless value.

The feed's exporters broke these here and there: gauges with _total, kilobits, percentages, milliseconds, labels that changed with the state and so started a new series. Each such name is fixed, and each fix is listed in Renamed metrics.

A service keeps its own prefix, dnsmasq_, wireguard_, unbound_, and OpenWrt's own metrics are node_openwrt_*. Where a widely used standalone exporter exists for a service and its names follow the conventions, they are taken too: letsencrypt's unbound_exporter, prometheus_wireguard_exporter, chrony_exporter. Someone who monitors Unbound on a server already has queries for those names.

docs.title: Modern names only
docs.text: There is no option to get the old names back. A compatibility mode would mean writing every metric twice, or picking names per device, and every query, dashboard and alert would have to know which. The cost of renaming is paid once, when moving from a feed exporter; carried as an option, it would be paid by every later change, every collector and every test, for as long as the option lived.

docs.title: The exporter's own
docs.text:
Every scrape ends with ucode_prometheus_exporter_build_info{version}, whatever collect[] selects, as node_exporter writes node_exporter_build_info. Its value is always 1; its version is the package's, 0.1.0-r1, or dev from a source tree. It answers "which version runs on that router?" from Prometheus alone, and a version change shows as a new series at the moment of an upgrade. It is named after the exporter, not node_, because it describes the exporter, not the node.

Beside node_exporter's node_scrape_collector_success and node_scrape_collector_duration_seconds, the exporter adds node_scrape_collector_observing: see About nothing to observe.

docs.title: About Nothing to Observe
docs.text: A collector can succeed, fail, or have nothing to observe. The third case exists because a device is not broken for lacking what it was never meant to have. This page is about where the line runs, and why it is drawn there.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: Install the -full group on an access point without DSL, or on a router whose dnsmasq someone disabled, and a scrape runs the DSL and dnsmasq collectors all the same. Before, those collectors failed: node_scrape_collector_success 0, every scrape, and a line in the log, every scrape. An alert on failing collectors then fires on every device that does not have everything, and gets silenced; the log fills with what the device is, rather than what went wrong; and a real failure, dnsmasq crashing on a router that runs it, looks exactly like the device that has no dnsmasq.

docs.title: The line
docs.text:
A collector whose subject is not there has nothing to observe; one whose subject is there and cannot be read fails.

  • Nothing to observe: hardware the device lacks (no radios, no DSL modem, no PoE switch), a kernel feature its kernel lacks (no connection tracking, IPv6 disabled), or a service someone disabled or never installed.
  • Failure: a service that is enabled and does not answer, a program that fails or runs out of time, a call or a file that is there and cannot be read or parsed.

A collector with nothing to observe succeeds: node_scrape_collector_success 1. It writes no sample, and the scrape logs nothing of it. What it does write is node_scrape_collector_observing{collector} 0, which is 1 for every other collector.

The service line follows what someone decided. A service whose init script is disabled was turned off on purpose: watching it is pointless, and complaining about it is noise. A service whose init script is enabled is meant to run: if it does not answer, something is wrong, and that is a failure.

docs.title: Why a metric of its own
docs.text:
Both a device without radios and a device whose radios have no clients write no Wi-Fi station samples, and both succeed. They mean different things: one cannot have clients, the other has none right now. node_scrape_collector_observing tells them apart, so a dashboard can show "no radios" instead of "0 clients", and an alert can ask for observing collectors only.

Folding it into node_scrape_collector_success was the alternative. It would keep one metric, but it would make "succeeded" mean two things, and break the node_exporter convention that dashboards rely on: success is whether the collector worked, and it did.

docs.title: Asking whether a service is enabled
docs.text:
Whether a service is enabled is what rpcd's rc object says: rc list with the service's name answers whether its init script is enabled, or that there is none. rpcd reads /etc/init.d and /etc/rc.d itself, outside the exporter's jail, so the jail needs nothing more than the ubus socket it already has.

A collector asks rc only once its own source fails. A running dnsmasq answers its own ubus call, and the scrape asks nothing more; only a call that fails costs a second one, to learn whether the failure is a failure. The exception is mwan3, whose ubus object is rpcd's own plugin, which answers whether mwan3 runs or not: there, rc is asked first. When rc cannot say, the failure stands: a failure that might not be one is still reported.

timesync asks procd instead: whether the instance of busybox ntpd or chronyd runs. sysntpd's init script is enabled on every image and starts ntpd only when the system's NTP client is turned on, so its enabled script says nothing; its instance does.

docs.title: Where to see why
docs.text:
The reason is not a label of the metric: a reason that changes would start a new series. It is where a person looks: service prometheus-exporter check, the ubus object's status (observing, reason) and LuCI's status page, as "dnsmasq is disabled" or "no wireless radios".

Each collector's cases, and the reasons it gives, are in Collectors.

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text:
• A disabled service is assumed to be on purpose. A service someone disabled by mistake is reported as nothing to observe, not as a failure. The alternative, treating every installed service as expected, would bring back the noise this exists to remove.
  • Hardware that disappears is not a failure. A USB modem unplugged, or a radio whose driver did not load, looks like a device without that hardware. node_scrape_collector_observing going from 1 to 0 is the signal to alert on, if that matters.

docs.title: Performance on Small Routers
docs.text: A scrape is a ucode program run on a router's CPU, and many routers have a slow one: a MIPS core of a few hundred MIPS, interpreting bytecode. This page is about what a scrape costs there, how that was measured, and where the cost still bites.

docs.title: The cost of the VM
docs.text:
Every operation of ucode's VM costs about a microsecond on a router: a loop's turn, a call of a builtin, a property read. A regex match costs several, and a regex literal is compiled each time it is evaluated. A scrape writes thousands of samples and reads tables of thousands of lines, so what matters is what is done per sample and per line.

That is why the code looks the way it does. Regexes are module constants, and kept out of what runs per line where index(), split() on a string or substr() do. A sample's line is written once, when it is recorded, and labels several samples share are written once and passed around. nat_traffic takes a conntrack line apart with fixed-string splits, without a regex or a function call per line. make bench shows what a collector costs, and holds the budgets of test/bench/budgets.uc: a scaling budget, a memory budget, and generous times.

docs.title: What a scrape costs
docs.text:
The same scrape, the typical world (a home router with Wi-Fi: 12 links, 300 conntrack entries, 20 stations, 50 leases) with the base package and the -full group, on each machine, with the speed of ucode's VM on it (calibrate:vm's loop turn) and of running a program:

Machine Typical full scrape A loop turn A program run devenv (Ryzen 7 7840U) 0.10 s 0.32 µs 1.7 ms NanoPi R3S (4×A55, OpenWrt 25.12.5) 0.55 s 2.0 µs 3.2 ms YunCore AX835 (MT7981, 2×A53 at 1.3 GHz) 0.72 s 3.0 µs 3.4 ms QEMU malta, 24Kc at 500 MIPS (QEMU_SHIFT=1) 2.0 s 9.9 µs 5.3 ms QEMU malta, 24Kc at 250 MIPS (QEMU_SHIFT=2) 4.0 s 19.7 µs

A scrape runs in a process of its own, as uhttpd answers each request in a process forked from the one that loaded the exporter, so it starts with nothing a scrape before left. The benchmark does the same: each run is a process of its own, timed after loading, and its memory is how far its peak rose above what it held before the run.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
A container limited to a share of one CPU stands in for a slower machine, when the share makes its loop turn match. On the laptop above, 0.35 of one CPU matched the R3S (2.0 µs, and 0.54 s for the scrape), 0.22 the AP (3.1 µs), and 0.07 the 500-MIPS 24Kc (10.7 µs), though not its scrape (3.4 s): a container's programs cost what the host's do under a quota, 30 ms a run there, while a router's cost what its own kernel makes them. The share depends on how loaded and how fast the host is, so it is picked in the same session as the run.

QEMU is the closer model of a MIPS router. It counts instructions (-icount shift=N,sleep=on, with the guest's clock on the same count), so its times are a deterministic function of the code and of N: shift 2 is exactly twice shift 1. A MIPS router's own speed is its clock times its instructions per cycle: an MT7621's 1004Kc at 880 MHz runs an interpreter at roughly 0.5 to 0.7 instructions a cycle, 450 to 600 MIPS, which is QEMU_SHIFT=1; a 24Kc at 600 to 750 MHz (QCA953x, QCA956x) at 300 to 450 MIPS, between shift 1 and shift 2. The A53 anchors the scale: a loop turn takes it 3.0 µs and the 1000-MIPS guest 4.9 µs, so it runs this code as a 1650-MIPS 24Kc would, three to four times an MT7621.

docs.title: Where it still bites: nat_traffic
docs.text:
nat_traffic reads the whole conntrack table, a line per connection, at every scrape. Its time grows with the table, linearly, as its scaling budget holds it to: 0.41 s for 20,000 entries in the devenv. A home router's table holds a few hundred entries; a busy one, or one under a flood of connections, tens of thousands.

Scaled by the loop turn, the 500-MIPS 24Kc is about thirty times slower than the devenv: 20,000 entries would take it about twelve seconds, more than Prometheus's default scrape_timeout of ten. That is an estimate, not a measurement: the benchmark's QEMU runs time the typical world, whose table is small. But the risk is plain. On a weak MIPS router with a large table, nat_traffic alone can make every scrape time out, and Prometheus then drops the whole scrape, not only nat_traffic's part.

It is in the -network and -full groups. On such a router, leave it out, disable it, or scrape it in a job of its own with a longer timeout; and watch node_scrape_collector_duration_seconds{collector="nat_traffic"}.

docs.title: Gzip
docs.text: A whole scrape of the lab (every collector, about 1250 series, on x86_64) is 143,500 bytes plain and 21,640 gzipped, 6.6 times smaller. Deflating it takes about 1 ms at zlib's fastest level, which the exporter uses, and 3 ms at its default level, for 19,160 bytes. Over loopback the scrape takes as long either way (118 ms plain, 123 ms gzipped): the gain is on the wire, 85% fewer bytes per scrape, which matters on a slow or metered link and costs the router little.

docs.title: Basic auth
docs.text:
The handler computes the password's hash in ucode at each scrape, so the hash's rounds are what a check costs (make bench's auth: cases, the median of a check in a process of its own):

Machine $1$ $6$, 1000 rounds (hash_password's) $5$, 2000 $6$, 2000 By the cache devenv (Ryzen 7 7840U) 2.5 ms 4.1 ms 6.5 ms 7.8 ms 0.09 ms NanoPi R3S (4×A55) 14 ms 19 ms 33 ms 37 ms 0.5 ms QEMU malta, 24Kc at 500 MIPS 63 ms 135 ms 206 ms 259 ms 2.4 ms

A round of SHA-512-crypt takes the 500-MIPS 24Kc 125 µs. The 9,999,999 rounds a hash may name would take it twenty minutes, the default 5000 0.63 s. So a hash takes at most 2000 rounds, a quarter of a second there, and more is refused. Even 1000 rounds are 135 ms of each scrape on such a router, which is why the handler keeps a cache of the last header it let in: a request it lets in by the cache costs about 2% of the full check, everywhere. See About the security model.

docs.title: About the Security Model
docs.text: The exporter runs as root, on a router, and answers requests from the network. It reads much of what the router knows: its interfaces and addresses, its clients and leases, its configuration. This page is about what keeps that from becoming more than a read, and the trade-offs taken along the way.

docs.title: A jail built from declarations
docs.text:
uhttpd, and the exporter in it, runs in procd's jail. The jail holds the exporter's own code and libraries, procfs, sysfs, the ubus socket and the log, and then what the installed and enabled collectors declare: the configs they read, the programs they run, the files and directories they read. Nothing else of /etc/config is there, and nothing outside it is writable but the exporter's small state directory.

The jail is computed, not written by hand. Each collector's meta says what it needs, the init script asks jail.uc what that adds up to, and procd mounts that. A collector the device does not install, or that its configuration disables, adds nothing. This is what makes the jail tight: it is exactly as wide as the collectors in use, and it stays right as packages come and go, without anyone keeping a list.

Some declarations are refused outright: a path that is not absolute or not plain, and directories that hold what every service has, /etc/config, /run, /tmp, /usr/lib and the like. A collector cannot ask for a socket in /run, because the jail would then hold every service's sockets. ujail cannot mount a socket by itself, so a collector names the socket's directory, which must be its service's alone, as Unbound's /var/lib/unbound is.

The jail is a boundary for the exporter's own mistakes as much as for an attacker's: a collector that parses something wrong cannot write anywhere, and one whose program hangs is killed with everything it started.

Read-only is not the same as harmless, so some files stay out of the jail whoever reads around them. /etc/config/network holds WireGuard's private keys: the wireguard collector does not declare it, and names peers by their descriptions only with peer_names, asking rpcd's uci object for the interface's peer sections alone and letting go of all but each one's public key and description. That keeps the keys out of the jail's files, where a mistake in reading a path could reach them; it is not a wall against an exporter that runs code it should not, which, as root with ubus, could ask rpcd for the whole config. The ubus object's interfaces, by contrast, asks netifd, so that a LuCI user allowed the exporter's object alone gets interface names without the file.

docs.title: What collectors get
docs.text: Inside the jail, a collector gets less than the jail holds. It receives capabilities, not modules: the fs functions that read and none that write; uci handles on the configs it named, read-only, of the committed configuration only, so a change staged in uci but not committed is never read; programs only from its own list, run without a shell's interpretation of their arguments, and killed with their children when its seconds are spent. See About the architecture.

docs.title: Basic auth, over TLS only
docs.text:
Basic auth sends the password with every request, encoded but not encrypted. Over HTTP anyone on the path reads it. So the exporter takes basic auth over HTTPS only: auth_user and auth_password without cert and key are an invalid configuration, refused wherever it is checked, start, reload, check, the ubus object's validate and LuCI alike. A configuration that asks for a login is never served without TLS, rather than served with a warning.

auth_password holds a crypt hash, never the password: the configuration, its backups and LuCI's forms never hold the secret. The ubus object makes the hash, so the password is not on a command line, where ps would show it. Neither the password nor the hash is logged, and no reply of the ubus object holds the hash.

docs.title: Why the handler checks the password itself
docs.text:
uhttpd has basic auth of its own: a config file of prefix:user:hash lines, -c, with a realm, -r. The init script writes that file, and uhttpd reads it. But OpenWrt 25.12's uhttpd applies it to files and CGI only, not to a handler's prefix: a request to /metrics would reach the handler without a login. uhttpd fixed this in August 2026 (commit 3aa7e1c), after every 25.12 release so far.

So the handler reads the same file when it starts, and checks every request against it before it scrapes, computing the hash in ucode as musl's crypt would. On a uhttpd that does check, the request is checked twice; on one that does not, it is checked once, which is what matters. A file that is there but wrong denies every request rather than letting them through.

docs.title: The cache, and what it trades
docs.text:
Computing a hash costs real time on a router's CPU: 135 ms for hash_password's 1000 rounds of SHA-512-crypt on a 500-MIPS MIPS core, at every scrape. And uhttpd's process per request keeps nothing in memory. So, after a request is let in, the handler writes to its state directory the SHA-256 of that request's exact Authorization header, bound to the user and the hash; a later request with the same header is let in on that digest, compared in constant time. Any other header pays the full check, and a wrong one stays out, leaving the entry as it was. A changed user or password lets nothing in by the old entry, and a restart forgets it.

The digest reveals no more than what is already on the device. It sits beside the hash, as closed: root's alone, in a directory of mode 0700 on tmpfs, never on flash nor in a backup. Finding a header that gives it is guessing the password, as with the hash, only cheaper per guess: one SHA-256 against a thousand rounds and more. That matters only to whoever can read the file, which is root on the router, who can also read the password itself from the next scrape, since uhttpd ends the TLS. A long random password, as a scraper's should be, is out of reach either way.

docs.title: Why the rounds are capped
docs.text: A $5$ or $6$ hash may name up to 9,999,999 rounds. A hash of that many would take a 500-MIPS router twenty minutes per scrape, and anyone who can set the configuration could make the exporter burn its CPU. So a hash may have at most 2000 rounds, a quarter of a second there, and a hash that names none, which means 5000, is refused like any invalid value. See Performance on small routers.

docs.title: Defaults that face inward
docs.text: The exporter listens on loopback until told otherwise: a fresh install exposes nothing. listen_interface takes a logical interface, so it follows that interface's addresses; *, every address, is a choice to make deliberately, since it includes the WAN's.

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text:
• The jail is not a sandbox against a hostile collector. It narrows what the installed collectors can reach; it does not vet them. A collector package is code you choose to run as root.
  • Outside the jail, things are wider. check, the ubus object's status and the prometheus-exporter command run outside it, as root, so that they can say what the jail lacks. chronyd's server statistics are read there and never in a scrape: reaching them means writing to chronyd's command directory, which the jail does not give.
  • rpcd runs the ubus object unjailed. It reads the committed configuration and writes nothing; hash_password alone handles a secret, and logs neither it nor the hash. The LuCI app's ACL grants the reading methods, and hash_password only to a login that may write.

docs.title: About Versioned Documentation
docs.text: The documentation describes a package that people install and then keep running for months. A router on last year's release should be able to read the docs of last year's release, and a reader who just arrived should land on the newest. This page explains how the publishing setup serves both, and why it is stricter than it first looks. The machinery itself is described in Documentation publishing.

docs.title: One version per minor, and only one maintained
docs.text:
The site has a folder per minor release, /0.1/, /0.2/, and /latest/ for the newest. Patch releases do not get their own folder; they overwrite their minor. A patch release changes behaviour in small ways at most, and a reader choosing between 0.2.0, 0.2.1 and 0.2.2 in a version selector gains nothing but a longer list. The title of each version still shows the exact release it was built from.

The exporter is a small project, and it maintains exactly one version: the newest. That shapes the docs too. Old versions stay online, because someone is running them, but they are frozen at their last publish. Only the newest version's docs get fixes. Backporting doc fixes to every old minor would be a promise the project cannot keep, and a half-kept promise is worse than a clear rule: a reader of /0.1/ knows it is a record of 0.1, not a living page.

The other half of the rule is that the docs of unreleased work are never published. main often describes behaviour no release has yet. Publishing it, even under a dev label, would put the most visible, most search-indexed pages ahead of the code people can actually install. So main and pull requests only build the site, strictly, to catch broken links early; they never publish it. The docs go online with the release they describe.

docs.title: Why the docs branches exist
docs.text:
A release tag is immutable, and so are the docs inside it. But the docs of a release will have mistakes: a typo, a wrong default, a missing step. Waiting for the next release to fix them leaves readers with the error for weeks, and cutting a release just for a doc fix spends a version number on something that is not a change to the package.

A docs/X.Y branch is the way out. It starts at the release tag, vX.Y.0, and carries doc fixes on top of it. Pushing it republishes /X.Y/. The branch is not a release branch and never becomes one: it exists only to let the published docs of a released version get better without a new release.

docs.title: Why the branch must stay docs-only
docs.text:
The danger of a branch that sits next to a release is that it slowly becomes one. A small code fix gets cherry-picked "just this once", the docs describe it, and now the published docs of 0.2 describe code that is not in any 0.2 package. Anyone reading them and running the real 0.2 sees something else. Worse, the branch now holds a version of the code that no tag names, and nobody can say which fixes it has.

The guard makes that impossible rather than discouraged. Before a docs branch publishes, it compares the branch with its release tag and refuses if anything outside the docs changed. The code in a docs branch is therefore always exactly the code of a release, and the only way to ship a code fix is a release, with a tag, a version number and a changelog entry. The refusal message says as much: "code fixes need a release".

The guard also insists that the newest release tag of the minor is an ancestor of the branch. After a patch release, the branch has to move onto the new tag before it can publish again. Otherwise a docs fix pushed to an old branch would overwrite the patch release's docs with the docs of the previous patch, silently undoing whatever the patch changed.

Tags are not guarded. A tag is the release; its docs are by definition the docs of that release.

docs.title: Why fixes go to main first, and why never rebase
docs.text:
A doc fix that only lands on the docs branch is lost at the next minor, which is cut from main. Landing it on main first and cherry-picking it onto the docs branch keeps main the one place every fix lives, and makes the docs branch a strict subset: its release, plus a few commits that are already on main.

Merging or rebasing main into the docs branch looks like a shortcut, but it brings along everything else on main, including the docs of unreleased features. The guard catches the code that comes with them, but not the docs, which it allows by design. Cherry-picking is deliberate: each commit that reaches a published version was chosen for it.

Merging a patch release's tag into the docs branch is a different thing. The tag is a release, so everything it brings has shipped. That is why moving the branch to a patch tag is a fast-forward or a merge, while main never goes in.

When the next minor ships, its branch takes over and the old one is frozen. Nothing stops a push to the old branch, but the one-maintained-version rule means there is no reason to.

docs.title: Why latest only moves forward
docs.text:
latest is what most readers see. It must always be the newest release, whatever order publishes happen in. Publishes do happen out of order: a fix to an older version, or a manual republish of one, can run after the newer minor has shipped. If every publish took latest, republishing 0.1 would silently point the whole site back at an old release.

So a publish takes latest only if its version is the newest one on gh-pages. The comparison is by version, not by text, because 0.10 is newer than 0.9 and a text sort says otherwise. Publishes also run one at a time, since two mike deploys racing on the same branch could each overwrite the other's work.

docs.title: Pinned links and latest links
docs.text:
A link to the docs is either about the project now or about a particular release. The README and a forum answer are about now: they should follow the project, so they link to /latest/. A changelog entry, a release note, or a URL inside the package is about one release, and has to keep pointing at the docs of that release after newer ones come out.

The package matters most. A router running 0.1 that shows a help URL should lead to the 0.1 docs, where the options and messages match what is installed, not to the newest docs, which may describe options it does not have. Pinning the shipped links to the package's minor gives every installed version a link to its own docs.

Pinned links rot silently: bump the version and forget one link, and the next release ships pointing at the previous minor. A check in make lint catches that. The changelog gets the same check per section, and [Unreleased] allows no pinned link at all, because the version it will be released as is not known yet.

Links between pages of the docs are always relative. A relative link resolves inside whatever version the reader is in, so each published version is self-contained without any rewriting.

docs.title: The redirect for old links
docs.text: A link without a version, /<site>/how-to/..., is an easy one to write by hand, and any link from before the site was versioned looks like that. Nothing lives at those paths any more. Rather than breaking every such link, the site's 404 page moves a missing unversioned path under /latest/, keeping its query and anchor. A path that is already inside a version folder is left as a real "not found": redirecting it could loop, and a page that does not exist in 0.1 should not quietly become a page of another version.

docs.title: Why mkdocs.yml stays free of mike
docs.text: The versioned settings live in their own file, mkdocs.mike.yml, which inherits mkdocs.yml. With the mike plugin and version provider in the main config, a plain mkdocs serve would show a version selector with nothing behind it, and every writer's preview would depend on mike. Keeping them apart means writing and previewing the docs needs nothing but MkDocs Material, and the versioned build is exercised on its own in CI and by make -C docs build-mike.

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text:
latest is a copy. mike can make an alias a symlink, a redirect page, or a copy. GitHub Pages cannot be relied on to serve symlinks, and redirect pages would make every /latest/ URL a hop through a stub. A copy gives real pages at stable URLs. The price is that every page of the newest version exists twice; the canonical URL of each page points to its /latest/ copy, so search engines can treat the two as one. Identical files are stored once in git, so the copy costs little on gh-pages.

The 404 redirect assumes a project site. It treats the first path segment as the site, which matches https://<user>.github.io/<site>/. On a custom domain or a user site, where the docs live at the root, the redirect would need changing.

CI and local builds use different installs. Local builds run the pinned mkdocs-material image, plus mike in a derived image. The publish job installs the same pinned mkdocs-material and mike with pip on the runner, which spares CI building the image, but their own dependencies are not pinned. A dependency release can therefore make CI's build differ from a local one. Both builds are strict, so the likely failure is a loud one, not a quiet difference in the published site.

The freeze is a rule, not a lock. Nothing technical stops a push to an old docs branch; the guard only keeps it docs-only. The project relies on the one-maintained-version rule for the rest.

docs.title: About Versions
docs.text: Releases are semantic versions, X.Y.Z, tagged vX.Y.Z. This page is about what each part promises to someone who builds on the exporter, and how the packages and the documentation follow the version.

docs.title: What a version promises
docs.text:
People build on the exporter in several ways: queries and dashboards on its metric names, scripts on its uci options and ubus methods, collectors on its collector interface, images on its package names. A version says which of those can break.

  • Major: a metric, label or metric type renamed or removed; a uci option renamed, removed or meaning something else; a ubus method's arguments or replies changed incompatibly; collect(deps, out, options) or meta changed incompatibly; a package or group renamed or split.
  • Minor: new collectors, metrics, labels on new families, options, ubus methods, and new cases of nothing to observe.
  • Patch: fixes, speed, and documentation.

A new case of nothing to observe is a minor change, though it changes what a scrape says of a collector: a collector that failed on some device now succeeds there, with node_scrape_collector_observing 0. Nothing that worked stops working, and an alert on failures fires less, for the right reason.

docs.title: Before 1.0.0
docs.text: Before 1.0.0, a minor version may break any of these, and says so. The project is young, the metric names and the configuration are still settling, and holding them fixed now would freeze mistakes. 1.0.0 is meant to be the first release to OpenWrt's packages feed, with the metric names and the configuration settled: from then on, a break is a major version.

docs.title: The package version
docs.text:
PKG_VERSION in the package Makefile is the release, 0.1.0. PKG_RELEASE, the -rN of 0.1.0-r1, counts changes to the packaging alone, a dependency or an install step, and starts again at 1 with each version. ucode_prometheus_exporter_build_info{version="0.1.0-r1"} reports both.

Every collector package, group and the LuCI app depends on the base package of the very same <version>-r<release>. A collector runs on the exporter's internals, and the LuCI app calls its ubus methods as that release has them; allowing a mix would mean testing every combination, and supporting the ones nobody tested. So an upgrade moves every package at once.

docs.title: The documentation's versions
docs.text: The documentation is published per minor release, /0.1/, /0.2/, with /latest/ for the newest, as About versioned documentation explains. A patch release replaces its minor's docs, since a patch changes no option, metric or method. A router on 0.1 reads the 0.1 docs, where the options and metrics are the ones it has.
